comment_body:
With async failure handling, ScheduleOne returns before the background goroutine finishes waiting on the status patch and calling sched.requeue(...).

Without ExpectUnschedulable: true, the test immediately advances to the PodGatedInQueue: "preemptor-mid-priority" step, which does an unpolled, immediate check (unschedulablePod(...) == nil) and flakes/fails because the pod has not finished requeueing yet.

Setting ExpectUnschedulable: true causes SchedulePod to poll until the pod actually re-enters the unschedulable pool before continuing. This matches the other preemption steps in this file (and line 1839 later in this same test).

+func TestTakeByTopologyNUMAPackedForResize(t *testing.T) {
+	logger, _ := ktesting.NewTestContext(t)
+	testCases := commonTakeByTopologyTestCasesForResize(t)
+
+	for _, tc := range testCases {
+		t.Run(tc.description, func(t *testing.T) {
+			strategy := CPUSortingStrategyPacked
+			if tc.opts.DistributeCPUsAcrossCores {
+				strategy = CPUSortingStrategySpread
+			}
+
+			result, err := takeByTopologyNUMAPackedForResize(logger, tc.topo, tc.availableCPUs, tc.numCPUs, strategy, tc.opts.PreferAlignByUncoreCacheOption, tc.reusableCPUs, tc.mustKeepCPUs)
+
+			if tc.expErr != "" && err != nil && err.Error() != tc.expErr {
+				t.Errorf("expected error to be [%v] but it was [%v]", tc.expErr, err)
+			}
+			if !result.Equals(tc.expResult) {
+				t.Errorf("expected result [%s] to equal [%s]", result, tc.expResult)
+			}
+		})
+	}
+}

comment_body:
goroutinesLimiter is an internal struct in pkg/scheduler/backend/api_dispatcher, so it would have to be exported/moved, and its name/design don't match what we do here:

We are not limiting goroutines: `finishFailureWithRequeue` / `finishFailureWithoutRequeue` already spawn the background goroutine so `scheduleOne` doesn't block; the limiter caps how many status patches can be in flight in apiCacher/apiDispatcher concurrently.

Single caller vs. many concurrent waiters: `goroutinesLimiter` is designed for a single caller (`APIDispatcher.run()`), so its `release()` calls `cond.Broadcast()` [goroutines_limiter.go:73](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1be627ab7e9819ac1d468b48de32142129afb7c2/pkg/scheduler/backend/api_dispatcher/goroutines_limiter.go#L68-L74) Here, many failure goroutines can be parked in acquire() at the same time - `Broadcast()` on every release would wake all of them for a single freed slot, whereas a buffered channel wakes exactly one waiter in FIFO order.

comment_body:
Thanks for looking at this.

With the gate on the container ends up not started after a restart regardless of this PR, by two separate paths. Once `AddPod` registers the worker, the existing worker lookup below already reports not started. And the worker is fresh, so its `containerID` is empty on the first `doProbe` and does not match the container the runtime still reports; with the gate on that branch seeds the result with `initialValue`, which is `Unknown` for startup (worker.go:296), and keeps it not started until a probe succeeds. The startup probe then runs again. Neither path depends on this change.

Pod readiness from `generateAPIPodStatus` for a container that survived the restart, written as `first sync after the restart` -> `the sync after that`:

| container at restart | gate | before restart | before this PR | after this PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| passed its startup probe | off | Ready | Ready -> Ready | Ready -> Ready |
| passed its startup probe | on | Ready | **Ready** -> NotReady | NotReady -> NotReady |
| still in its startup period | off | NotReady | **Ready -> Ready** | NotReady -> NotReady |
| still in its startup period | on | NotReady | **Ready** -> NotReady | NotReady -> NotReady |

Row 1 is the case you raise, on the default gate, and it is untouched: the `Started` short-circuit returns before the new check, so the container keeps Started and the pod stays Ready.

Row 3 is what this PR is for. The pod stays Ready for good, because `Started` is preserved across syncs and `worker.doProbe` stops probing once it is set, so the startup probe never records a result that could correct it.

Rows 2 and 4 end NotReady either way. What goes away there is the Ready the first sync published before the worker was registered, which is what #135795 reports, where it lasted long enough for a PodDisruptionBudget check to pass and let an eviction through.

So the new check does not cause the re-probe or the NotReady. It stops the first sync after a restart from reporting a container as started while its startup probe has not passed.

Happy to take this over, per [the Slack thread](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0409NGC1TK/p1790005963450609).

I gave the synctest rewrite a go first, but it turns out locking a `sync.Mutex` is explicitly [not durably blocking](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.27.1/src/testing/synctest/synctest.go#L86-L91), so the bubble never notices the deadlock. Against the unfixed controller the test just sits there until `go test` kills it, which is worse than the 1s timeout we started with.

So I went a different way: the handler [probes `ctrl.mutex.TryLock()`](https://github.com/harche/kubernetes/blob/2560ad7c304b07f2c3fa9be31c5c27f39f14336a/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/resourceslice/resourceslicecontroller_test.go#L1895-L1903) before re-entering `Update`. Nothing else runs concurrently in the test, so if the probe fails, `Update` must still be holding the lock. No goroutines, no timeout, and it fails instantly without the fix.

Full diff against master, original commit untouched and the test change in a second one:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/compare/master...harche:kubernetes:dra-resourceslice-update-errors

If you'd rather keep the goroutine and just bump the timeout to 5s, that's easy too, though it's still a guess and takes the full 5s to fail when it does. Let me know and I'll open the PR.
